summary: A Network Host Status report covering July 3 to July 14, 1972. Testing was skipped on July 4 for the holiday and on July 11 and 12 because the author was away. It was replaced by RFC 370.

eli5.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: A snapshot of which ARPANET computers were working in mid-July 1972.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed to track which hosts on the ARPANET were reachable and ready to serve users, so traffic could be routed efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: Ellen Westheimer at BBN ran daily connectivity tests from the BBN Terminal IMP to each network host, recording whether each opened a connection, was dead, timed out, or was in use.
tldr.outcome: The report provided operators a detailed view of network availability during early July, helping them understand where services were available.

facts.label: Status codes used
facts.value: O, D, T, H, F, R

today: RFC 367 is a historic document superseded by RFC 370. It records ARPANET operational status during mid-July 1972.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC reports on the status of ARPANET host computers from July 3 to July 14, 1972. Testing was skipped on July 4 (Independence Day holiday) and July 11-12 (the author was on vacation).

The report explains which hosts were included in daily testing and which ones were excluded because they were user-only machines or Terminal IMPs not expected to host services.
sections.eli5: This is a checklist of which big computers on the network were working during mid-July, skipping a few days when no one was there to check.

sections.title: Excluded Hosts
sections.content:
Terminal IMPs at AMES, MITRE, RADC, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, NOAA, and SAAC were excluded because they were user-only machines, not servers. The Network Control Center (address 5) was also excluded because it only gathered statistics. Additionally, Rand (7), Harvard (73), Lincoln TSP (138), Illinois (12), NBS (19), and USC (23) were designated as users-only and not included in regular testing.

This distinction meant the network had different expectations for these machines: they were clients using network services, not providers of services to others.
sections.eli5: Some machines were excluded because they were just using the network for themselves, not offering services to other machines.

sections.title: Test Results
sections.content:
BBN's Terminal IMP tested each host multiple times during the testing days. Status codes included: O (Open: connected and accessible), D (Dead: unreachable), T (Timed out: no response within 60 seconds), H (1/2 Open: connected but closed immediately), F (Full: host said all ports were in use), and R (Refused: host rejected the connection).

The results show typical patterns: reliable hosts like MIT-Multics were open most days, while others like AMES-67 and CASE were dead nearly every day tested.
sections.eli5: The test marked each computer with letters: O meant it was awake, D meant it was off, and other letters showed different problems like the computer being too busy.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 370, which continued the weekly network status tradition. Host status reports remained a regular feature of ARPANET operations.
sections.eli5: This report was just for two weeks. Later reports kept coming out regularly to help network users find available computers.

references.text: Westheimer, E., "Network Host Status", RFC 370, August 1972.
